data.name: Holodrive
data.detailed_description:
A high-speed 2D multiplayer shooter where you design and customize your robot. Gear up, jetpack around, and race to victory!

Jump in - It's Free to Play, now with Cocoball!

Holodrive is free to play, and you don’t need to spend a dime to keep things fair. You can collect all combat items just by playing! Dive into Deathmatch or try one of the three team-based modes, including the new Cocoball, for a cluckin' good time!

The Rise of the Explosive Dummies

When Holocorp made the Dummies, they intended them to be the ultimate companion robots—man's new best friend. Who knew they’d end up obsessed with blowing each other up in style? Now, decked out in flashy gear and armed with guns and wild power-ups, these robots battle it in crazy arenas to prove who's the best. What could go wrong?

Non-Stop Multiplayer Action

The action in Holodrive is fast, strategic, and packed with explosions! You'll quickly get into the groove of blowing each other up, and when you do, you'll respawn in no time to keep the chaos going. Use the map to your advantage—teleport into the thick of the fight or duck behind anti-bullet barriers to surprise your enemies!

Become a Weapon Collector

You can carry up to 7 weapons at once. Scavenge weapons and ammo as you navigate the levels, or grab them from the enemies you take down. Score new weapons by opening packs, crafting them, or snagging the free weapon that rotates every 3 days!

Mobility, Versatility, Unpredictability

Every Dummy comes with a jetpack, letting you zip around the arena with speed. The fast-paced action is enhanced by ramps and power-ups placed strategically, adding an element of surprise that can instantly change the game.

Customize and Show off your Stylish Self

Customize everything from your hat to your jetpack! Open Holopacks to get complete sets like Shinobi or Ninja, or mix and match parts to make a bold fashion statement that stands out in the arena.

reviews.review:
Holodrive is an energetic 2D multiplayer shooter that combines arena combat with platforming-style mobility, weapon collecting, character customization, and a deliberately humorous presentation. Developed by BitCake Studio and published by Versus Evil, it revolves around customizable robots called Dummies that use jetpacks, firearms, explosives, and power-ups to tear through compact arenas. Its concept is straightforward, but the emphasis on movement and environmental interaction gives the action considerably more personality than a basic side-scrolling deathmatch game.

Movement is arguably the most distinctive part of the experience. Every Dummy has a jetpack, allowing players to quickly reposition themselves, attack from unexpected angles, escape dangerous encounters, and move vertically through the stages. Ramps and strategically positioned power-ups add further opportunities for sudden changes in momentum. The arenas themselves are not merely decorative spaces either. Teleporters can throw players directly into another confrontation, while anti-bullet barriers provide temporary protection and can be exploited to surprise opponents. Consequently, learning a map becomes an important skill rather than simply memorizing where enemies are likely to appear.

Combat follows the same philosophy of constant activity. Death is followed by a quick return to the battlefield, preventing matches from becoming bogged down by long periods of inactivity. Weapons and ammunition are scattered around the maps and can also be taken from defeated opponents. A player can carry as many as seven weapons simultaneously, creating considerable flexibility during a fight. Instead of committing to a single firearm or rigid class, players can accumulate a miniature arsenal and switch their approach depending on the situation. Additional weapons can be acquired through packs and crafting, while the rotating free weapon system provides another way to expand the available selection.

The multiplayer modes help prevent all of this mobility and weapon variety from being restricted to straightforward elimination. Deathmatch provides the obvious arena-shooter foundation, but three team-oriented modes broaden the structure, with Cocoball being one of the more distinctive options. Team play gives movement, positioning, map knowledge, and coordination greater importance because simply accumulating eliminations is no longer necessarily the entire objective. Cross-platform multiplayer is also listed among its Steam functionality, although the experience remains fundamentally dependent on having other players available.

Its free-to-play design is comparatively sensible in concept because combat equipment is intended to remain obtainable through normal gameplay. Players are not supposed to need purchases simply to access the tools required to compete. Optional purchases exist, but progression through matches, packs, crafting, and weapon collection remains central to the structure. This approach is particularly appropriate for a competitive game, where locking meaningful battlefield advantages behind mandatory payments would undermine the appeal of improving through practice.

Customization supplies much of the game's personality outside combat. Hats, jetpacks, clothing pieces, and themed cosmetic sets can be combined to create distinctive Dummies. Complete appearances such as Ninja and Shinobi sets are available, but individual components can also be mixed together. It fits the intentionally absurd premise in which robots originally conceived as companions somehow became obsessed with blowing one another apart while dressed in increasingly elaborate outfits. The narrative is little more than playful background flavor, but that is appropriate for a game primarily concerned with immediate multiplayer action.

Visually, the colorful 2D and 2.5D presentation complements the frantic mechanics. Clear platforms and environmental features are important when players are simultaneously jetpacking, collecting equipment, avoiding gunfire, and tracking opponents. The cartoonish robots and exaggerated combat also prevent the constant explosions from becoming overly serious. The presentation establishes a recognizable identity without distracting from the information players need during fast encounters.

The largest drawback comes from its multiplayer dependence. There is little reason to approach it expecting a substantial solo adventure or story-driven campaign. Its maps, weapons, cosmetics, crafting, modes, achievements, and progression systems ultimately exist to support repeated competitive matches. This also means the quality of the experience is closely tied to the availability of other players. For an older online title, population becomes an especially important practical consideration, and players should recognize that even strong multiplayer mechanics lose much of their usefulness when matchmaking activity is limited.

Steam Deck compatibility is another area requiring caution. The Steam store currently lists Windows as the supported operating system and does not provide an official Steam Deck compatibility rating for the game. As a result, it should not be treated as officially Verified or Playable on Steam Deck. Running it through Proton may be possible, but because the experience depends heavily on online functionality, prospective Deck users should regard compatibility as unofficial and potentially inconsistent rather than expecting a guaranteed plug-and-play handheld experience.

There is nevertheless a genuinely enjoyable design underneath those practical limitations. Jetpacks make traversal satisfying, rapid respawning maintains momentum, environmental mechanics reward map knowledge, and carrying multiple weapons encourages improvisation. Cosmetic customization gives players something personal to pursue, while team modes provide alternatives to standard deathmatch. The result is an appealing mixture of platforming movement and arena shooting that feels particularly suited to short, chaotic multiplayer sessions.

As a complete package, Holodrive has plenty of charm and several clever ideas, especially in the way mobility, weapon collection, environmental features, and customization interact. Its greatest weakness is not necessarily the underlying design but its reliance on an active online environment and the absence of officially confirmed Steam Deck support. For players who can find matches and enjoy fast arcade shooters where movement matters as much as aiming, it remains an entertaining and distinctive take on competitive 2D action. 

Rating: 7/10
